tool.name: AspectZonalStatisticsAsTable

summary.para: Summarizes an aspect raster per zone into a table of circular statistics: mean direction, resultant length, mean resultant length, circular variance and standard deviation, angular variance and deviation, median direction, circular range, von Mises concentration, the Rayleigh test of uniformity, and the 95% confidence interval of the mean direction. Very similar to Esri's Zonal Statistics as Table tool, but targeted specifically at aspect rasters -- and it requires no Spatial Analyst or Image Analyst extension.

tool.usage:
Relation to the Esri tool. This tool deliberately mirrors Esri's Zonal Statistics as Table (Spatial Analyst / Image Analyst): zones come from an integer raster or from features, all cells sharing a zone value are summarized together, and the result is a standalone table with one row per zone. The Esri tool's own Calculate circular statistics option gives the same mean direction and circular standard deviation as this tool's MEAN_DIR and CIRC_SD (identical values from the same cells), but it treats flat cells (-1) as an angle of 359 degrees, so flat ground pulls every zone toward north; this tool leaves flat cells out and counts them, interpolates the aspect at point zones, and adds the mean resultant length, variances, angular deviation, median, range, von Mises concentration, Rayleigh test and confidence interval. It differs in three ways. First, every statistic is circular: aspect is a circular variable (0 and 360 degrees are the same direction; 359 and 1 are two degrees apart), so the ordinary zonal MEAN and STD are simply wrong for it -- the linear mean of 359 and 1 is 180, due south, the exact opposite of the correct answer. Second, the options that do not apply to circular data (percentiles, multidimensional processing, the output join layer) are omitted; there is no "calculate circular statistics" checkbox because circular statistics are the entire point. Third, it needs no extension: everything is computed internally, so it runs on any ArcGIS Pro license.
Zones. All features sharing the same value in the zone field -- or all raster cells sharing the same integer value -- form one zone, and the statistics summarize every aspect cell belonging to that zone. Zone rasters must be integer rasters and must share the aspect raster's coordinate system. Feature zones are processed one zone at a time, each over its own window of the aspect raster, so zones that overlap are each analyzed in full (the current Esri Zonal Statistics as Table behaves the same way; earlier versions rasterized the zone features first, and an overlapped polygon lost the overlapped portion of its area). On a feature layer with a joined table, the joined fields are offered as zone fields under their qualified names. Within a single zone, overlapping features count each cell once.
How cells are gathered. Polygon zones use every aspect cell whose center falls inside the zone. Polyline zones use every cell the line passes through. Point zones interpolate the aspect at each point as a bilinear weighted mean direction from the four surrounding cell centers: each neighbor's unit vector (sine and cosine) is weighted by the ordinary bilinear weights and the resultant converted back to a direction, so a point surrounded by cells at 358, 359, 1 and 2 degrees interpolates to roughly 0 (due north), never 180. Flat and NoData neighbors are excluded from the interpolation with the weights renormalized; a point whose neighbors are all flat counts as flat.
Flat cells. A flat cell (aspect = -1) faces no direction at all, so it cannot participate in directional statistics; including it as a number would poison every statistic. Flat cells are therefore excluded from the calculations -- the tool says so when it runs -- but they are never silently discarded: each zone's flat cells are counted in the FLAT_COUNT field and reported as a percentage of the zone in FLAT_PCT, so a zone that is mostly flat announces itself.
Statistics. The Statistics type list offers all the circular statistics the Polar Plots tool reports, or all of them at once (the default). COUNT (directional cells used), FLAT_COUNT and FLAT_PCT are always written. Mean direction, resultant length and mean resultant length (r-bar) come from the vector sum of the unit vectors; circular variance (1 - r-bar), angular variance, circular standard deviation and angular deviation are the standard dispersion measures; the median direction and circular range are order statistics computed on a fine 0.1-degree histogram; the von Mises concentration (kappa) follows Fisher (1993) / Best and Fisher (1981); the Rayleigh Z and p test the null hypothesis of no preferred direction, with p from Zar (1999) equation 27.4, the same formula Topography along Lines uses; and the 95% confidence interval of the mean direction uses the von Mises large-sample standard error 1 / sqrt(n * r-bar * kappa) (Fisher 1993), reported as a half-angle plus lower and upper bounds. The Rayleigh test and the interval both assume independent observations. Neighboring raster cells face nearly the same way, so for polygon and polyline zones almost any zone tests significant and the interval is much narrower than the real uncertainty -- read it as a lower bound. When a zone's cells are all the cells in the zone, the mean direction is a census value and needs neither. Point zones spaced farther apart than aspects stay correlated (plots, random samples) can be independent, and then the test and interval mean what they say.
Input checks. The aspect raster may be any pixel type, but the tool inspects it and warns when something suggests it is not an aspect raster: values outside the -1 to 360 range, or geoprocessing history indicating a D8 flow-direction raster (whose codes are categories, not angles). D-infinity flow-direction rasters are directional data in the mathematical convention (0 = east, counter-clockwise); the input-convention drop-down converts them to compass, and it defaults automatically from the raster's geoprocessing history (Compass when nothing can be determined). If Ignore NoData is unchecked, any zone containing a NoData aspect cell receives NULL statistics, matching the Esri tool's behavior.
The output table's metadata records the inputs and settings (provenance), and the tool prints a ready-to-run Python snippet so the run can be scripted. No Spatial Analyst or Image Analyst extension is required. Circular statistics follow Mardia and Jupp (2000), Fisher (1993), Batschelet (1981) and Zar (1999); see also Jenness (2012), "Issues with directional data."

param.name: in_zone_data
param.displayname: Input raster or feature zone data

dialogReference.para: The zones: an integer raster (each distinct value is a zone) or a point, polyline, or polygon feature class or layer. An active selection on a layer is honored. Overlapping features in different zones are each analyzed in full; overlapping features in the same zone count each cell once.

The field defining the zones: features sharing the same value form one zone. Integer, text, GUID, and ObjectID fields are all accepted (choosing the ObjectID makes every feature its own zone). Required for feature zones; a zone raster always uses its cell value (the field defaults to Value).

The aspect raster to summarize: compass degrees 0-360 with -1 meaning flat, as produced by Esri's Aspect or Surface Parameters tools. Any pixel type is accepted. Values outside -1 to 360 trigger a might-not-be-an-aspect-raster warning and are excluded. D-infinity flow-direction rasters are supported via the input-convention setting below.

The output table: one row per zone, holding the zone value, COUNT (directional cells used), FLAT_COUNT and FLAT_PCT, and the chosen circular statistics. A name is suggested from the zone dataset; the suggestion can be cleared or changed. A table written to a folder rather than a geodatabase becomes a dBASE table: the tool adds the .dbf extension and writes -999 for any statistic it cannot compute for a zone, because a dBASE table cannot hold NULL.

Checked (default): NoData aspect cells within a zone are simply skipped and the statistics use the remaining cells. Unchecked: any zone containing a NoData aspect cell receives NULL statistics (the Esri tool's behavior with the same setting).

Which circular statistic to write, or All circular statistics (the default) for every one of them. COUNT, FLAT_COUNT and FLAT_PCT are always included. The choices are the statistics reported by the Polar Plots tool:

bulletList.bullet_item: Mean Resultant Length (r-bar) and Resultant Length
Circular Variance, Angular Variance, Circular Standard Deviation, Angular Deviation, and Circular Range
the 95% Confidence Interval of the mean direction (half-angle plus lower and upper bounds)

dialogReference.para: How the raster encodes direction. Compass (the default): 0 = north, increasing clockwise -- ordinary aspect. Mathematical: 0 = east, increasing counter-clockwise -- the convention of D-infinity flow-direction rasters, which are essentially aspect (the direction of steepest descent); directions are converted to compass before the statistics. The setting defaults automatically from the raster's geoprocessing history and falls back to Compass when nothing can be determined. Dispersion and concentration statistics are identical under either convention; only the direction-valued outputs (mean and median direction, CI bounds) depend on it.

scriptExample.title: Aspect Zonal Statistics as Table (Python)
scriptExample.para: Summarize an aspect raster by watershed polygons, all circular statistics.
scriptExample.code: import arcpy # The .pyt ships next to the add-in; ImportToolbox registers alias "jenness". arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") arcpy.jenness.AspectZonalStatisticsAsTable( in_zone_data=r"C:\data\project.gdb\watersheds", zone_field="WSHED_ID", in_raster=r"C:\data\project.gdb\aspect", out_table=r"C:\data\project.gdb\watersheds_AspectZonal", ignore_nodata=True, statistics_type="All circular statistics", input_convention="Compass (0 = north, clockwise)")

dataIdInfo.idAbs: Zonal circular statistics for aspect rasters: the circular analog of Esri's Zonal Statistics as Table (https://doc.esri.com/en/arcgis-pro/latest/tool-reference/spatial-analyst/zonal-statistics-as-table.html), computed without any Spatial Analyst or Image Analyst extension. References: Mardia, K.V. and P.E. Jupp. 2000. Directional Statistics. Wiley (https://doi.org/10.1002/9780470316979). Fisher, N.I. 1993. Statistical Analysis of Circular Data. Cambridge University Press (https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511564345). Batschelet, E. 1981. Circular Statistics in Biology. Academic Press. Zar, J.H. 1999. Biostatistical Analysis, 4th ed. Prentice Hall. Best, D.J. and N.I. Fisher. 1981. The bias of the maximum likelihood estimators of the von Mises-Fisher concentration parameters. Communications in Statistics - Simulation and Computation 10(5):493-502 (https://doi.org/10.1080/03610918108812225). Jenness, J. 2012. Issues with directional data. Remotely Wild, newsletter of the Spatial Ecology and Telemetry Working Group of The Wildlife Society.
dataIdInfo.idPurp: Summarize an aspect raster per zone with circular statistics, as a table.
